one_liner: Relaxed std::atomic fetch_add on a shared counter in place of a std::mutex-guarded increment; teaching idiom, not a library.
what_it_does: A book example (Chapter_05/5x01-atomic_flag.cpp) that times three ways for 4 threads to bump one shared uint32_t: std::mutex lock/unlock around counter++, a hand-written std::atomic_flag test-and-set spinlock, and atomic_counter.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed). The takeaway is an idiom: when a mutex guards nothing but one integer, make the integer a std::atomic and drop the lock.
how_it_is_fast: The atomic increment is one hardware read-modify-write on the counter's cache line, so there is no lock acquire/release pair, no separate mutex word to bounce between cores, and no sleep/wake path when threads collide. Under contention the mutex adds lock handoffs and blocking on top of the cache-line ping-pong both variants pay, which is why the gap grows with thread count. memory_order_relaxed requests atomicity only, with no ordering of surrounding memory.
when_to_use: Statistics, hit, byte or progress counters updated from many threads and read occasionally, where nothing else has to change together with the count.
Reference counts, ID or ticket generators where a single fetch_add (using its returned old value) is the whole critical section.

Code that takes a std::mutex only to protect one integer: per the book's Table 5.1 as relayed in the record, the atomic is cheaper even uncontended (0.82 s against 1.03 s for 200 million increments on one thread).
Moderate contention on a counter that cannot be sharded, where the book's 2-4 thread figures show the mutex falling 2.2-2.7x behind.
when_not_to_use: Critical sections that update more than one variable or keep an invariant (counter plus container, check-then-act): an atomic counter does not protect them, so keep the mutex.

Very hot counters hit by many threads: the atomic still serialises on one cache line. From the book figures, 4 threads doing 800 million increments took 9.13 s, about 2.8x longer than one thread at its 0.82 s per 200 million pace would need for the same total (derived from those figures); per-thread or sharded counters summed on read avoid this.
When other threads must observe data written before the increment (publishing results, completion flags): relaxed gives no ordering, so use release/acquire or the default seq_cst.

Counter types the platform cannot update lock-free: std::atomic of a large type silently uses an internal lock (the repo's 5x04-atomic_type_not_lock-free.cpp shows a 512-byte struct reporting is_always_lock_free false), which removes the advantage.

integration.dependencies: none for the idiom (<atomic>); building the repo's example tree needs Boost 1.86 (thread, system, container), GoogleTest and {fmt} at the root, and Chapter_05 links libatomic
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 for std::atomic and memory orders; the repo targets C++20/23 with GCC 14.2 or Clang 18
integration.platforms: any platform with lock-free 32-bit atomics; repo README lists Linux (Ubuntu 24.04), macOS Sonoma and Windows 11
integration.thread_safety: fetch_add is safe for concurrent callers; memory_order_relaxed orders nothing else, so a reader can see the new count before the work it counts
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — one-for-one only when the mutex guards a single integer update; reads become atomic loads, and any multi-step critical section still needs the lock

gotchas: The checked-in file does not reproduce the book table like-for-like: the mutex loop runs 200000000 increments per thread but the spinlock and atomic loops run 500000000, with NUM_THREADS fixed at 4; divide by 2.5 or edit the loops before comparing printed times. Each variant is a single run with thread creation inside the timed region and no warm-up.
The root CMakeLists.txt sets no default build type and adds -O3 -DNDEBUG only for Release, so a plain cmake configure builds the benchmark without optimisation flags; pass -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release.
The file uses std::mutex and uint32_t without including <mutex> or <cstdint>, relying on transitive includes of the standard library it was written against (other standard libraries not checked).
The companion spin_lock is a bare test_and_set loop with no backoff or pause instruction; it is a teaching foil, not a lock to copy.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Same idiom as the sibling 'The Art of Writing Efficient Programs: std::atomic counter increment' entry (book figure 23 ns against 7 ns on one thread); this one adds 2- and 4-thread points and a spinlock middle option, so read both, copy neither harness. The queue siblings (atomic_queue, moodycamel, Boost.Lockfree, xenium) solve message passing; use this idiom when the shared state is a single integer.
verified_claims_summary: The book's Table 5.1, relayed by the seed lead and not in the repo, times 200 million increments per thread of one shared counter: relaxed fetch_add 0.82 s, 4.52 s and 9.13 s against std::mutex 1.03 s, 10.15 s and 24.61 s at 1, 2 and 4 threads, about 1.3x, 2.2x and 2.7x (derived from those figures). No CPU, compiler version or flags come with the table, and the repo's checked-in harness (single std::chrono run, unequal loop counts) does not regenerate it as is.
status_note: MIT-licensed book companion code (95 stars, 34 forks, not archived); this file last changed 2024-09-08 ('Cleaning and fixing unwanted warnings') and the 2026 commits only edit a README banner, so treat it as frozen teaching code and copy the three-line idiom rather than the harness.
